title: More isn't more (Avot 2:7)
hook: more flesh, more worms; more possessions, more worry; more Torah, more life

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hillel spoke to a skull on the water, and warned about the circle of revenge. Your line was harm comes back. Did you let a small hurt stop with you? Day two hundred fifty-six.

The shoes, the gadget, the bigger apartment: the thing someone really wanted, finally bought. For a few days, it was wonderful. And then, quietly, it came with things. A password to remember. A warranty to register. A thing to insure, to clean, to worry about being scratched. A rented storage unit is a monument to this feeling. Hillel noticed it too, and turned it into a saying with a beat. It sounds almost like a chant.
screen: `THE THING YOU REALLY WANTED.` → `IT CAME WITH THINGS.` → `A SAYING LIKE A CHANT.`

segments.voice: Here's how Hillel's list begins. More flesh, more worms. More possessions, more worry. It's blunt. A body fattened on luxury ends in the same grave as everyone else's. And the more you own, the more you have to guard. In Hebrew it has a beat: marbeh nekhasim, marbeh de'agah. More things, more worry. The list goes on through the households of his ancient world, with a few lines about servants and wives that read uncomfortably today, and are honestly part of the text. And then the list turns. More Torah, more life. More sitting in study, more wisdom. More counsel, more understanding. More tzedakah, more giving to those in need, more peace. See what Hillel's doing. He isn't against more. He's saying some kinds of more shrink you, and some kinds of more grow you. Possessions pile up and need guarding. Wisdom, understanding and generosity pile up and set you free. And the list ends with a surprise about generosity. Giving looks like it should leave a person with less. Hillel says it leaves you with more peace. Then he adds one more line: a person who has gained a good name has gained it for himself, but a person who has gained words of Torah has gained life in the world to come. A good name is precious, he seems to say, but it stays here. What you learn and give goes further. So the carry is short: more isn't more. The question is always: more of what?
screen: `MORE FLESH, MORE WORMS.` · `MORE THINGS, MORE WORRY.` · `THE LIST TURNS: MORE TORAH, MORE LIFE.` · `MORE GIVING, MORE PEACE.` · then, large: `MORE ISN'T MORE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one thing to let go of. Settle, and breathe. Picture walking slowly through your home. A closet. A drawer. A shelf. Look for one thing you're keeping that you don't need, and that someone else could use. A coat. A book. A pan. Notice the small tug of wanting to keep it. Then picture it in someone else's hands, being useful. See if the tug loosens. The bell holds the time.
Marbeh de'agah. More possessions, more worry: the beat of Hillel's list, before it turns to more learning, more life, and more giving, more peace.
Your line: more giving, more peace. Today, give one thing away, and notice whether you end up with more worry or more peace. Day two hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: Giving tzedakah, charity understood as justice, is a central Jewish practice, and some households keep a tzedakah box and drop coins in before Shabbat.

original.note: Mishnaic Hebrew: more possessions, more worry.

trapdoor: what you thought: stuff is bad.
what it means: some kinds of more shrink you and some grow you, so ask more of what.
what a scholar hears: the list runs on one repeated word, marbeh, more, and turns halfway from things to Torah, wisdom and tzedakah.

notes: Avot is paraphrased (outline follows Taylor 1897). Numbering: 2:7 common, 2:8 in some editions.
The script names but does not recite the lines about wives, maidservants and manservants; a Keeper may prefer a different handling.
'Every storage unit in America' is a light image, not a statistic.
